items.note: A considerable portion of the north and north-east of Madhya Bharat follows the course of the Betwa; river systems and mountains are said to have shaped history and culture.
The Bhilsa tract (north-eastern plateau) encircled by wooded Vindhyan ranges was always prosperous, reflected in the richness of its monuments.
Region called Dasharna in ancient geography; the name survives in the Dashan stream flowing into the Betwa; ancient Vidisha and later Bhilsa the focal point.

items.note: Western Hindi with Bundeli in the north of Madhya Bharat; Malwi (southern Rajasthani) once used across the plateau but now reported by few.
A branch of the Haihayas ruled at Vidisha (Bhilsa), which is next only to Mahishmati in antiquity in Central India.
Prince Ashoka married a daughter of a Vidisha banker; he laid the foundations of the Sanchi stupa and raised a monolithic pillar close to it.
Agnimitra as viceroy at Vidisha (Malavikagnimitra); Heliodoros Garuda pillar at Besnagar as ambassador of Antialcidas to Bhagabhadra, embracing the Bhagavata sect.
Vidisha as a centre of orthodox faith and of a great cultural and art movement represented by monuments near Bhilsa and Sanchi.
Simuka Satavahana is said to have conquered districts round Vidisha; early Satavahana coins suggest Malwa within their influence.
Nasik prashasti of Gautamiputra lists Anupa, Akara (east Malwa) and Avanti (west Malwa) among his conquests.
Regions about Gwalior and Bhilsa under the Nagas, ruling from Kantipuri, Padmavati and Vidisha; copper coins found at Kotwal and Pawaya.
Samudragupta's Allahabad Pillar Inscription claims victory over the Nagas and the Sanakanikas near Bhilsa; Madhya Bharat under one sceptre under the Guptas.
Footnote: more than a dozen images of Saptamatrikas, Durga, Kubera recovered from Besnagar; and a Sanakanika Maharaja vassal of Chandragupta II excavated a cave near Udayagiri (Bhilsa).
Prosperity under the Guptas reflected in monuments at Besnagar and Udaygiri (Bhilsa); Besnagar antiquities unique in Gupta classic art.
Besnagar antiquities important for early Vaishnavism and Shaivism: colossal Durga, Seven Mothers, Nrisimha, Vishnu, Ekamukha lingas.
Eastern plateau near Bhilsa for a time under the Rastrakutas; Pathari pillar inscription of 861 A.D. records a pillar erected by a minister of Parabala.
Paramaras, formerly Rashtrakuta feudatories in Gujarat, shifted to Malwa; Siyaka II perhaps the first independent Paramara ruler.
Bhoja (1010-1050 A.D.) called the greatest Paramara monarch; greatness rests more on patronage of art and literature.
Fallen fortunes of the family revived for a time by Udayaditya (1058-1087) and his successor.
Loss of Paramara territory incl. Ujjain to Siddharaja Jay Singh; Arjunavarman (1211-1215) last able prince; Muslim invasions ended Paramara rule.
Malwa's art and architecture praised for magnificent temples at Udaypur, Nemawar, Jamli, Badnawar and Un (sentence continues on next page).
Malwa under the Paramaras produced a rich galaxy of literary magnates; its fame in Sanskrit learning largely due to Bhoja.
Bhoja rebuilt Dhara; Kamal Maula's mosque said to have been the great college known as Bhoja Shala.
Iltutmish marched against Malwa and first captured the fort of Bhilsa before reaching Ujjain.
